punctuation_present: sometimes — periods and question marks appear in some sentences (e.g. 3, 7, 8) but many utterances end without any mark (e.g. 1, 5, 6)
register: spontaneous conversational speech (casual spoken narrative/interview transcript with self-corrections and hesitations)
non_boundary_traps: -고 (frequently chains actions, not a full stop)
근데 at clause-medial position (resumptive, not always a new turn)
trailing 그런데/그래도 fragments that attach forward
target_language_risks: Korean drops subjects/objects freely; a fragment translated alone in English will need an inferred pronoun or subject that may be wrong without later context
Sentence-final particles and honorifics (e.g. -시-, -어요) carry politeness/aspect info that is lost if segmented too early
Left-branching relative clauses and topic markers (은/는) mean the topic established early governs a verb far later, so premature segmentation forces English word order guesses
Self-repairs and repeated words (e.g. '두 두') can be mistranslated as meaningful repetition if segmented mid-repair
Head-final verb endings determine tense/aspect/modality; cutting before the verb loses this and produces incomplete English clauses
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is unedited spoken Korean with frequent self-repair, trailing connectives (-는데, -고, -어서), and optional punctuation, so segmentation must rely on morphological clause-final endings rather than punctuation alone. Treat connective endings as strong signals to hold the segment open until the following clause resolves, and never split right after a filler or a repeated stutter token. Because Korean is strictly head-final and pro-drop, delay emission until the main verb/ending of a clause is visible to avoid mistranslating dangling arguments in English.
